The implications of the early phases of human telencephalic development,
involving neural stem cells (NSCs), in the etiology of cortical disorders remain
elusive. Here, we explore the expression dynamics of cortical and neu-
ropsychiatric disorder-associated genes in datasets generated from human
NSCs across telencephalic fate transitions in vitro and in vivo. We identify risk
genes expressed in brain organizers and sequential gene regulatory networks
throughout corticogenesis, revealing disease-speciﬁc critical phases when
NSCs may be more vulnerable to gene dysfunction and converging signaling
across multiple diseases. Further, we simulate the impact of risk transcription
factor (TF) depletions on neural cell trajectories traversing human cortico-
genesis and observe a spatiotemporal-dependent effect for each perturbation.
Finally, single-cell transcriptomics of autism-affected patient-derived NSCs
in vitro reveals recurrent expression alteration of TFs orchestrating brain
patterning and NSC lineage commitment. This work opens perspectives to
explore human brain dysfunction at early phases of development.
The mammalian cerebral cortex emerges from the dorsal tele-
ncephalon, where organizing centers secrete morphogens that
instruct the spatiotemporal identity of neural stem cells (NSCs)1–5.
Radial glial (RG) cells serve as NSCs, ﬁrst generating excitatory gluta-
matergic neurons which migrate to the cortex, later becoming
gliogenic6–10. The cerebral cortex is also populated by inhibitory γ-
aminobutyric acid (GABAergic) interneurons, originating primarily
from ventral telencephalic NSCs, that migrate dorsally and integrate
with excitatory neurons11,12.
Disruption of these events by germline and/or somatic muta-
tions, or environmental insults, may lead to malformations of cor-
tical development (MCDs) and neurodevelopmental disorders

Dysfunctional neuronal mechanisms during late gestation or
postnatal life have been associated with cortical and neuropsychiatric
disorders24–31. However, several works suggest the disruption of NSC
functions as earlier fetal risk events32–38. Despite their importance, the
implications of early NSCs in the etiology of brain diseases and the
impact of their dysfunctions on postnatal brain remain elusive. As it is
challenging to explore these early phases of human development, it is
necessary to employ pluripotent stem cell (PSC) models, which reca-
pitulate patient-speciﬁc corticogenesis in vitro, including sequential
generation of neurons and glia34,39–43.
Here, we curated gene lists associated with MCDs and NDDs, and
explored their expression through the progression of human NSCs
(hNSCs) exploiting in vitro and in vivo brain datasets. We identiﬁed
critical phases for each disorder, deﬁned as distinct NSC states during
human telencephalic development that are more vulnerable to gene
disruptions. Moreover, we identiﬁed transcription factor (TF) net-
works along hNSC progression, revealing convergent genes shared
among diseases and disorder-speciﬁc interactions. We then used Cel-
lOracle to simulate the impact of TF disruptions on neural cell lineages
spanning human corticogenesis. Using autistic patient-derived cell
lines, we uncovered frequent expression alteration of brain patterning
and NSC fate regulators across donors. This study demonstrates that
brain disease-associated genes may be functionally relevant during
early development, suggesting that disrupted telencephalic patterning
and NSC events contribute to multiple disorders.
We created a resource to explore disease gene expression in neural
cells across the datasets that we used, accessible at NeMO/genes.
Results
Enrichment of cortical disorder risk gene expression in human
telencephalic cells
We compiled lists of genes associated with MCDs, including micro-
cephaly (MIC), lissencephaly (LIS), cobblestone (COB), heterotopia
(HET), polymicrogyria (POLYM), hydrocephalus (HC), focal cortical
dysplasia (FCD), mTORopathies (mTOR), and NDDs, including schi-
zophrenia (SCZ), attention deﬁcit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD),
major depressive disorder (MDD), bipolar disorder (BD), autism
spectrum disorder (ASD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD),
Tourette syndrome (TS), developmental delay (DD), as well as neuro-
degenerative disorders, such as Alzheimer’s (AD) and Parkinson’s dis-
eases (PD) (see methods; Supplementary Dataset 1).
These diseases encompass cortical alterations commonly asso-
ciated with neuronal dysfunctions24–31. To map the expression patterns
of these risk gene sets in the early fetal human brain, we performed
expression-weighted cell type enrichment (EWCE) analysis on single-
cell RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from telencephalic regions
spanning the ﬁrst trimester44 (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a, b). Con-
sistent with our previous ﬁndings in macaque brain37 and other
studies24,26,27, genes associated with NDDs were enriched in both inhi-
bitory and excitatory neuronal signatures. Similarly, LIS, FCD, and
dyslexia genes showed neuronal enrichment, while MIC- and HC-
associated genes were enriched in RG cells and glioblasts, MIC-,
POLYM-, and rare MCD-associated genes in intermediate progenitor
cells (IPCs), and AD genes in immune cell signatures.

neurogenesis in vitro leveraging a bulk RNA-seq dataset, generated

patterns (p1-12) depicting transcriptomic progression of the cells

associated genes in these patterns showed most of the gene lists

(Supplementary Fig. 2c).
However, we have recently shown that many neuropsychiatric
disorder-associated genes, while globally enriched in neurons, are also
expressed in early telencephalic organizers (also called patterning
centers, PCs) and NSCs, during macaque corticogenesis37. Consistent
with these ﬁndings, most brain diseases showed at least 50% of their
associated genes expressed in human RG cells of the ﬁrst trimester44,
with the highest proportion for MCD, DD, and ASD (Fig. 1bi). This
analysis demonstrates that many cortical disorders commonly asso-
ciated with neuronal dysfunction involve risk genes active already in
NSCs during early human telencephalic development.
Given the limitations of distinguishing precise NSC states with
human brain primary data, we compared these ﬁndings with our pre-
viously established in vitro model, where human (h)PSC-derived
forebrain NSCs were serially passaged and exposed to varying doses of
the mitogen FGF2 to assess their differentiation potential at each stage
of their progression (Supplementary Fig. 3a)40. This assay, hereafter
referred to as the “NSC progression protocol”, demonstrated that
dorsal hNSCs transitioning from pluripotency spontaneously recapi-
tulate early phases of telencephalic development, including a state
resembling the cortical hem, the dorsomedial-posterior organizer,
before becoming neurogenic. We analyzed bulk RNA-seq data along
the in vitro progression of these hNSCs and found that they expressed
a similar proportion of risk genes as primary human RG cells, sug-
gesting that in vivo transcriptomic dynamics are paralleled in vitro40
(Fig. 1b, Supplementary Fig. 1c). Thus, we further employed this in vitro
system to assess putative roles of risk genes in NSCs during early
human telencephalic development.
Previous RNA-seq analysis identiﬁed 24 GWCoGAPS patterns
(p1–p24), describing transcriptomic dynamics across this in vitro hNSC
progression40 (Supplementary Fig. 3b; NeMO/CoGAPS). Here, we
focused on those patterns speciﬁc to discrete NSC states triggered by
FGF2 doses and passage (PS, Fig. 1ci). Projection analysis48 of single-cell
(sc) and microdissection expression data of primate developing
neocortex37,49–51 matched the in vitro hNSCs of each passage to their
in vivo equivalent cell types (Supplementary Fig. 3b–d). Therefore, we
further annotated hNSCs as neuroepithelial/organizer progenitors at
early passages (PS2-3), excitatory neurogenic RG at mid passage (PS4),
and late neuro-/glio-genic RG at late (PS6-8) passages (Fig. 1cii), com-
plementing our previous ﬁndings40. We interrogated the expression of
the disease gene sets throughout the progression of hNSCs and found
differential enrichment over distinct phases. For instance, MIC-
associated genes were enriched at early neuroepithelial and mid-
neurogenic states, HC genes from early neuroepithelial stem cells
(NESCs) to late RG cells, while LIS, mTOR, and SCZ risk genes in mid-
and late-RG cells (Fig. 1d). Analysis of a similar in vitro dataset52 yielded
congruent ﬁndings, highlighting risk genes enriched in hNSCs and in
the derived neurons and glia (Supplementary Fig. 2d–f). These results
indicate that NSCs play critical roles in early cortical disorder events
that can be further dissected using this human in vitro system.
Expression dynamics of risk genes across human cortical NSCs
progressing in vitro
We ordered genes within each disease gene sets by their average
expression peak across the progression of the in vitro hNSCs40,
revealing disease-speciﬁc distributions of the risk genes (Fig. 1ei,
Supplementary Fig. 4ai–wi; NeMO/genes and NeMO/diseasegenesets).
For instance, MIC-speciﬁc risk genes involved in cell replication, such
as ASPM and CENPJ, were highly expressed in the ﬁrst passages (PS2-3),
suggesting that the earliest founder cells of the telencephalon may be
more vulnerable to cell cycle machinery perturbations than later RG
cells. HC-associated genes, also highly expressed in PS2-3, included key
regional identity regulators, such as ARX, FGFR3, and GLI337,53,54,

Expression dynamics of risk genes across mammalian neuro-
genesis in vivo
To assess the expression dynamics of risk genes during the progres-
sion of cortical NSCs in vivo, we leveraged a mouse scRNA-seq dataset
in which apical RG cells were proﬁled at high temporal resolution
across sequential differentiation stages (1, 24 and 96 hours) towards
cortical glutamatergic neurons at each embryonic day (E), from E12 to
E1557. We determined a slope of expression change for each gene
through differentiation (Fig. 1eii, Supplementary Fig. 4aii–wii), then
summarized the result binning the expression change for each gene
set (Fig. 1gi). These results highlight expression of risk gene sets in RG
cells and during their differentiation in vivo for all the disorders. Early
diseases, e.g. MIC and HC, exhibited a higher proportion of genes in RG
cells from E12 to E15, unlike later disorders, e.g. ASD and LIS, which
showed a higher proportion of genes in the differentiation phase.
We next explored risk gene expression dynamics across neuronal
maturation exploiting the DeCoN resource58, where mouse cortico-
thalamic (CThPN), sub-cortical and cortico-spinal motor (ScPN), and
interhemispheric callosal (CPN) projection neurons were proﬁled by
RNA-seq from E15.5 to postnatal day (P)1. We determined a slope of
expression change for the risk genes from immature to mature state of
each neuron subtype (Fig. 1eiii, Supplementary Fig. 4aiii–wiii), then
summarized their distribution in disease-speciﬁc bins (Fig. 1gii). Genes
associated with COB, MIC, HC, HET, and ASD (HC65 and S1) were
highly enriched in immature neurons. In contrast, diseases such as
ADHD and SCZ exhibited more genes with higher expression in mature
neurons. While most diseases showed consistent patterns among all
neuronal subtypes, some exhibited subtype-speciﬁc biases, such as
COB-associated genes, whose expression decreased speciﬁcally during
SCP maturation. Moreover, while each disease encompasses genes
with increased or decreased expression trends in RG-to-neuron or
immature-to-mature neuron transitions, all diseases included genes
expressed in both trajectories, suggesting multiple critical phases in
the pathogeny of these cortical disorders (Fig. 1g). Together, these
data conﬁrm the implication of brain disorder-associated risk genes
across the progression of RG cells and in neuronal transitions during
in vivo corticogenesis.
Finally, we assessed the enrichment of two ASD-associated risk
genes, the RNA-binding protein FMRP and chromatin remodeling
factor CHD8, and their targets identiﬁed from mouse and human brain
datasets, in our disease gene sets and DisGeNET (Supplementary
Fig. 5a, b; Supplementary Dataset 2). While FMRP and CHD8 targets
were enriched in ASD- and DD-associated genes, as expected, they
extended to other disorders depending on the brain tissue stage, fetal
or adult, where they have been identiﬁed. This analysis of the tran-
scriptional intersection of FMRP and CHD8 with their targets ascer-
tained in different brain phases and neural cell types suggests roles in
both disease-speciﬁc and -shared developmental pathways, including,
but not restricted to, ASD.
Disease risk genes expressed in telencephalic organizers
We checked whether risk genes have a dorsal or ventral bias during
telencephalic development, exploiting our previously reported bulk
RNA-seq data from six hiPSC lines throughout differentiation into
forebrain NSCs and neurons40, an assay hereafter referred to as the
“neuronal differentiation protocol” (Fig. 2ai). Transcriptomic analysis
identiﬁed gene expression patterns (GWCoGAPS p1-30) distinguishing
hPSC lines more prone to form dorsoposterior (DP) or anteroventral
(AV) telencephalic organizer states in their transition from plur-
ipotency, with divergent bias to generate glutamatergic or GABAergic
neuronal lineages, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 25ci). Here, we
further validated this lineage bias by projecting these patterns onto the
PCs from our recent macaque developing brain dataset37 (Supple-
mentary Fig. 6a; NeMO/CoGAPSII). The analysis consistently dis-
tinguished dorsal- versus ventral-biased lines, expressing cortical hem
or rostral patterning center (RPC, an AV organizer) genes, respectively,
at day in vitro (DIV) 8. Then, we analyzed the enrichment of each
disease risk gene list throughout the differentiation of these hNSC
lines, i.e., at DIV 8 when the organizer states emerge, and later in
neurons at DIV17 and 3040 (Fig. 2a; Supplementary Dataset 3). Diseases
were sorted by the proportion of dorsal-biased genes at DIV8. For
instance, HET risk genes showed a dorsal bias at all phases, unlike COB
genes which were enriched early in the AV organizer state and later in
dorsal excitatory neurons, suggesting multiple spatiotemporal risk
phases. Genes associated with ASD, ADHD, HC, and FCD appeared
early in both ventral- and dorsal-biased NSCs, and later in the derived
neurons.
Next, we assessed whether risk genes expressed in hNSCs at the
organizer state in vitro (DIV8) were present in telencephalic organizers
in vivo, leveraging our macaque37 and mouse59 developing brain
scRNA-seq datasets, where PCs have been proﬁled at high resolution
(Fig. 2b, Supplementary Fig. 6b, c). Neural fate regulators such as
FOXG1 and MEIS2, associated with ASD, showed ventral bias in vitro
and an equivalent expression in the AV organizers [i.e., RPC (PC FGF17),
AV (PC NKX2-1), and ganglionic eminence (GE, RG NKX2-1)] in vivo. In
contrast, EMX2, associated with Neuroticism, exhibited a dorsal bias
in vitro and was expressed in the cortical hem clusters [(PC RSPO3) and
hem/choroid plexus epithelium (CPe, PC TTR)] in vivo. Several early
genes (e.g., MEIS2, ARX, and FOXG1) became later expressed also in

Temporal gene networks throughout human NSC progression
in vitro
Other TFs, while not currently classiﬁed as risk factors, may still
interact with disease genes contributing to the pathobiology of a
disease. Employing RcisTarget, we determined “temporal-speciﬁc”
regulons for all the genes peaking at each hNSC phase, without
requiring core TFs to be disease-associated or their targets to co-
occur in a disease gene list. We identiﬁed 60 temporal regulons and
assessed their enrichment for disease genes (Fig. 3d; NeMO/
TempRegulons). Since the targets in temporal regulons differ
from those in the disease set, this analysis identiﬁed a distinct set of
core TFs with little overlap with those disease-associated, limited to
MTF1, SIN3A, TAF1, PURA, and MECP2. Regulons in PS4 low FGF2
and PS8 high FGF2 contained a high number of targets and were
shared among diseases (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Fig. 8e). For exam-
ple, the core TF MTF1 associated with ASD, putatively targeted
genes at PS4 enriched in other disorders, including Fragile X Mes-
senger Ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1) associated with HET, AUTS2 and
MECP2 associated with DD, and cannabinoid receptor 1 (CNR1)
associated with FCD (Supplementary Dataset 5). However, the
heightened connectivity at PS4 and PS8 could result from shared
binding motifs among promiscuous core TFs. Clustering binding
motifs identiﬁed a prominent cluster of Krüppel-like family (KLF/SP)
TF motifs at these NSC phases (Supplementary Fig. 9a–c). Despite
mutually exclusive targets of these TFs at PS4 and PS8, diverse sets
of disease-associated risk genes were enriched in KLF/Sp targets. By
contrasting disease and temporal regulons, we identiﬁed multiple
KLF/SP family members in both (Fig. 3a, d). Together, our regulon
analyses reveal molecular mechanisms shared across diseases,
identifying target genes where multiple disruptions might converge
during NSC progression, and unique disease-speciﬁc pathogenic
signaling60,61.
In silico assessment of gene regulatory network disruption
across human corticogenesis
The convergent or divergent expression dynamics of TFs and targets
suggest varying severity for a perturbation during neurogenesis,
depending on the TF-target’s role in a network and functioning
timing. This raised the need to investigate the effect of gene network
perturbations across different phases of human neurogenesis. We
leveraged single-cell multiomic (RNA-seq and ATAC-seq) data from
the developing human cortex of four donors, spanning post-
conceptional week (PCW)16 to 24, reported in Trevino et al.62.
Using CellOracle, we reconstructed cell type-speciﬁc gene regulatory
networks (GRN)63 and simulated the effect of perturbations of TFs on
neural trajectories through distinct phases of corticogenesis. To gain
higher resolution in NSC subpopulations, we reanalyzed the Trevino
et al.62 dataset including markers from monkey37 and mouse57 single-
cell studies. This distinguished multiple NSC states, including ven-
tricular early (vRG E) and late (vRG L), outer early (oRG E) and late
(oRG L), and truncated (tRG) radial glial subtypes, as well as their
glutamatergic neuronal and glial progeny (Fig. 4a and Supplemen-
tary Fig. 10; Supplementary Dataset 6).
Unlike RcisTarget, CellOracle constructs networks based on TF-
target co-expression and chromatin co-accessibility. Furthermore, to
be susceptible to perturbation, a TF must pass thresholds of
expression levels and variance across cells. This ﬁltering yielded 141
TFs, including 61 disease-associated, perturbable in at least one cell
trajectory (Supplementary Fig. 11). We applied CellOracle to each cell
subtype across RG progression and gliogenesis from all donors
(PCW16-24), to derive transcriptomic trajectories spanning the entire
spectrum of NSCs and glial cells (RG progression/gliogenesis).
Additionally, we constructed GRNs through neurogenesis from
individual donors at PCW20, 21, and 24, each capturing complete RG-
to-neuron trajectories, which served as biological replicates (Sup-
plementary Fig. 11). Transcriptomic complexity and GRN con-

Then, we systematically compared the impact of each KO simu-
lation on individual cell-type fate transition across both trajectories
(Fig. 4e, f, Supplementary Figs. 16, 17). Among these, KO of KLF4, which
peaks at PS8 and is present in both trajectories, depleted vRG cells
favoring transitions to SVZ states (oRGs), reduced both mGPCs, pro-
moting astrogenesis, and nIPCs enhancing neurons, with less effects
on differentiated cells. KO of ARX and HES1, both peaking at PS2 and
present in the neurogenic trajectory, depleted RG cells and nIPCs
incresing neurons (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 17). Applying Cel-
lOracle to a mousedeveloping cortex dataset64 and each human donor,
demonstrated similar perturbation-induced cell transitions across
species and donors strengthening our predictions, with some excep-
tions (e.g. FOXP1) likely reﬂecting methodology for dataset generation
or species differences. These results suggest that TF disruptions have
cell state-restricted effects.
We further categorized the TFs by their connectivity within the
networks in each cell type, from ultra-peripheral, i.e., isolated, to
kinless hub, i.e., highly involved in the network (Fig. 4e, f, Supple-
mentary Figs. 16, 17). For example, while KLF6 emerged as a hub in all
cell types spanning RG progression/gliogenesis and neurogenesis,
KLF4 was peripheral in most cells in both trajectories. EOMES (PS2)
was peripheral in the glial lineage but became a hub in neurons.
These analyses provide a functional map of the TFs deﬁning their
roles through NSC progression, neurogenesis, and gliogenesis.
Altogether, these data emphasize the context-speciﬁc effects of a
lesion13 and predict “risk spatiotemporal-domains” for each TF net-
work perturbation across cortical development.
Individual-speciﬁc critical phases in ASD patient-derived NSCs
Our in vitro hNSC models enable analysis of patient-speciﬁc disease-
associated molecular features during very early telencephalic devel-
opment. We generated NSCs from iPSCs of three idiopathic ASD
patients (#375, #384, and #434) and three controls (#290, #311, and
#317), differentiated them into neurons applying the neuronal differ-
entiation protocol, and performed scRNA-seq at DIV 8 (Supplementary
Fig. 25b; Supplementary Dataset 8). Unsupervised clustering, aided by
curated cell-type markers derived from our monkey brain dataset37,
identiﬁed a predominant population of early NESCs/RG cells (RGEarly)
and smaller clusters of late RG cells (RGLate), mesenchymal cells (Mes),
neurons, and brain organizer progenitors with predominant anterior
neural ridge/RPC-resembling cells (PC FGF17-like). We excluded cells
with a high fraction of mitochondrial genes or coupled with uncertain
markers, resulting in 44,311 high-quality cells for downstream analysis
(Fig. 5a, Supplementary Fig. 19).
NSCs derived from ASD patients displayed a higher proportions of
cells in G1 phase, suggesting enhanced commitment to neurons65
(Supplementary Fig. 20). We grouped RGEarly cells by cell cycle phase
and donor, creating donor-balanced pseudobulk samples. Principal
component analysis (PCA) of gene expression revealed high PC6 in
ASD versus control samples (Supplementary Fig. 21a). Then, projection
of the passaged hNSC dataset40 into this ASD-associated PC6 indicated
the highest level in the neurogenic NSCs of PS4 (Supplementary
Fig. 21b), aligning with the more distinguished ASD critical phase
(Fig. 1f). Next, using DESeq2, we identiﬁed 1259 differentially expressed
genes (DEG) between ASD and controls, including 131 TFs (absolute
logFC >0.5 and adjusted p-value < 0.05) (Fig. 5b; Supplementary
Dataset 9). Notably, many telencephalic patterning genes were
deregulated in ASD-derived NSCs. DP identity genes, such as WLS,
RSPO2, EMX2, and FEZF2, were decreased, while RELN and AV genes,
including FOXG1, as previously reported33, and ZIC1 were upregulated.
To explore individual contributions to these gene expression
differences, we performed analysis of DEG in RGEarly cells from each
ASD line versus the grouped control lines. We identiﬁed 75 up-
regulated (11 TFs) and 50 down-regulated (12 TFs) genes in ASD NSCs
(23 TFs in total), exhibiting donor-speciﬁc expression variation (Fig. 5c;
Supplementary Dataset 10). Notably, ASD#384 showed upregulation
of AV patterning regulators (FOXG1, MEIS2, and SIX3), and down-
regulation of DP regulators (DMRTA1, EMX2, and WLS), while ASD#434
exhibited enhanced HES4, HES5, and WNT7B, and decreased DLK1,

differentiation day 0 (TD0), distinguishing ASD lines with low AV
organizer and high cortical hem gene expression from those with
opposite pattern (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Fig. 22a). However, we
found less pronounced differences in the expression of cortical
regional markers (frontal, motor-somatosensory, occipital, and tem-
poral) (Supplementary Fig. 21e). These ﬁndings suggest more com-
promised dorsoventral than frontotemporal axis patterning in ASD-
affected telencephalons.
We observed high recurrence of the DEG identiﬁed in RGEarly of
our ASD lines within the DEG detected across the organoid NSC
subtypes (RG-hem, RG, tRG, and oRG) of the ASD-control pairs from
Jourdon et al.34, which was more pronounced for the TFs (Fig. 5e;
Supplementary Fig. 22a–c). Notably, most of the 23 TFs differentially
expressed in the RGEarly cells in our lines (Fig. 5c), including the NSC
fate regulators POU3F2 and LHX2, were frequently deregulated
(upregulated or downregulated) also across the multiple families,
especially at TD0 (Fig. 5f), exhibiting variation in the direction of
change among the pairs (Supplementary Fig. 22d). Immunohis-
tochemistry validated the expression of POU3F2, the nucleic
acid–binding protein YBX3, DMRTA1, LHX2, HES1, and FEZF2 in
germinal zones and AV or DP regions of the early macaque tele-
ncephalon, denoting a role for many of these genes in NSCs beyond
their recognized neuronal function6 (Fig. 5g, Supplementary ﬁg. 23).
Notably, many of these 23 TFs exhibited no or limited expression in
late gestation and postnatal human cortex66,67, further suggesting a
function restricted to early development (Supplementary Fig. 24).

jection of the ASD-associated PC6 from scRNA-seq of our lines in this
bulk data showed high levels in ASD NSCs again in the critical PS4
(Supplementary Fig. 21a and c; NeMO/PCA). These ﬁndings indicate
persistent regulatory alterations in ASD NSCs throughout cortical

We recreated CellOracle networks for each trajectory to include
selected TFs ﬁltered out in the previous analysis, such as DMRTA1,
EMX2, FOXG1, LHX2, and MEIS2, and simulated loss-of-function effects
for each of these 23 TFs on individual cell lineages traversing human
corticogenesis (Fig. 5h, i). Many perturbations had pleiotropic effects,
such as POU3F2 KO, which promoted early vRG maturation and mGPC
differentiation while hindering neurogenesis, whereas HES4, HES5 and
FEZF2 KOs induced RG maturation and neuron transition impacting
less gliogenesis. Notably, HES4 emerged as a hub in late RG and mGPCs
during gliogenesis, but in all cells during neurogenesis. These ﬁndings
further underscore the context-speciﬁc effect of a TF depletion across
NSC trajectories in complex disorders such as ASD. In conclusion,
these data demonstrate the potential of our in vitro modeling when
integrated with in vivo datasets, to uncover vulnerable phases unique
to each individual’s neurodevelopment and phenotypic diversity
within brain disorders.
Discussion
We explored the pathobiology of a broad range of cortical disorders
in NSCs traversing early phases of human brain development,
revealing potential disease mechanisms with diverse onsets and
genetic architectures. Building on previous observations in macaque
brain37 and integrating our in vitro human NSC models40, which
recapitulate telencephalic patterning, neurogenesis, and gliogenesis,
with human and cross-species developing brain datasets, we identi-
ﬁed disorder-associated genes expressed in early organizer centers
and in NSCs. These ﬁndings suggest an earlier fetal origin of these
disorders than previously recognized24–31, implicating dysfunctional
patterning events and NSC fate transitions during human brain
development. Each disease gene set exhibits a distinct dynamic
pattern during NSC progression and differentiation revealing speciﬁc
critical phases, vulnerability periods when most risk genes are highly
active and disruptions may yield more pronounced effects. For
example, MIC shows an earlier putative onset in NSCs than FCD,
consistent with previous studies23, while HC, linked to cerebrospinal
ﬂuid homeostasis disfunctions70, includes genes expressed in orga-
nizers, suggesting impaired patterning and fate speciﬁcation of
early NESCs.
The regulon analysis predicts TF cross-interactions throughout
the progression of cortical NSCs, revealing distinct pathogenic net-
works within a disease, as well as single genes converging into a
broader network implicated in multiple disorders60. Our analyses
“size” the role of a TF in a network, that may function as a hub in one
regulon or a peripheral target in another, reﬂecting its relevance in the
critical phase and the cell-restricted etiology of a disease. Thus, the
impact of a mutation might depend on when and in which cell type it
affects a gene function during brain development13,21,27,31 as well as on
the genomic context71.
The in silico perturbation analysis predicts the effects of TF loss of
functions on discrete cell transitions, in sequential spatiotemporal
contexts during human corticogenesis. The analysis reveals how dif-
ferent gene alterations can impact shared lineage trajectories, poten-
tially causing similar dysfunctions in distinctdisorders. Conversely, the
same loss-of-function at different developmental stages can lead to
divergent outcomes and symptoms in individuals carrying the same
genetic variant. Thus, the GRN analyses reveal critical phases for
disease-related TFs in early NSCs and across corticogenesis, suggest-
ing cell-type-speciﬁc effects of perturbations and candidate mechan-
isms underlying brain development and dysfunction.
Notably, we identiﬁed KLF TFs, implicated in brain development
and disorders72, linking multiple regulons in neurogenic and late NSCs
in vitro. Consistently, these TFs exhibit the highest connectivity among
neural cells in vivo, as previously reported73, suggesting a role as
master regulators in corticogenesis. Therefore, our ﬁndings help in
identifying key risk TFs, modeling and comprehending phenotypic
heterogeneity within a disorder and overlapping features of diverse
diseases.
We retrospectively explored early neurodevelopment in indivi-
duals with idiopathic ASD, assessing donor-derived NSC lines with
our in vitro system, and integrating a larger dataset of ASD-
organoids34 and primate brain data37. We identiﬁed deregulation of
telencephalic organizer genes and neural fate regulators, including
FOXG1, MEIS2, and POU3F2, whose deleterious variants have been
already linked to ASD by genomic studies74–76. Complementing these
works, we now provide a time frame during human brain develop-
ment when perturbations of these genes can contribute to the dis-
ease onset. Building on previous studies correlating ASD pathology
to NSC dysfunctions32–34, we hypothesize that compromised pat-
terning and spatiotemporal identity instruction of telencephalic
NSCs by dysfunctional organizing centers may be among the earliest
causes of altered proliferation rate, neurodevelopmental trajec-
tories, and neuron type imbalance2,3 in idiopathic ASD. Further work
is required to establish causality between these TF alterations and
clinical phenotypes. However, our loss-of-function simulation across
human corticogenesis predicted more critical effects in NSC phases.

tions in multiple genomic contexts and explore phenotypic varia-
bility in neural trajectories in a larger pool of donors71,77. Notably, the

Compilation of brain disease risk gene lists
We collected lists of genes associated with MCDs, including micro-
cephaly (MIC), lissencephaly (LIS), cobblestone (COB), heterotopia
(HET), polymicrogyria (POLYM), hydrocephalus (HC), focal cortical
dysplasia (FCD), rare MCDs, mTORophaties (mTOR), and develop-
mental dyslexia (Dev. Dyslexia) from literature20,36,38,78–87. From GWAS
datasets, we collected gene lists associated with NDDs including
schizophrenia (SCZ)88,89, attention deﬁcit hyperactivity disorder
(ADHD)90, major depressive disorder (MDD)91, bipolar disorder
(BD)92, neuroticism (NEUROT)93, autism spectrum disorder (ASD)75,
anorexia nervosa (AN)94, the neurodegenerative Alzheimer’s (AD)95
and Parkinson’s diseases (PD)96, and intelligence quotient (IQ)97.
Genes related to developmental delay (DD) from the Deciphering
Developmental Disorders Study consortium98 were collected as well.

ADHD, AD, AN, ASD, BD, IQ, MDD, NEUROT, PD, SCZ, Tourette

Heatmaps of Fig. 1d were created using the heatmap() function in

Expression-Weighted Cell Type Enrichment Analysis in Braun
et al.44
We performed expression weighted cell type enrichment (EWCE)
(package version 1.13.1)102 to identify which cell types show signiﬁcant
enrichment for disease-associated genes in the ﬁrst-trimester data
from Braun et al.44. In accordance with the EWCE pipeline, scRNA-seq
counts were normalized and variance-stabilized using the sctransform
package (version 0.4.1)103. EWCE’s bootstrap enrichment test was
applied separately for each selected subregion and each develop-
mental stage in the Braun et al.44 dataset. We used 10,000 permuta-
tions (n_reps = 10000), and the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method
(mtc_method = “BH”) for multiple-testing correction. All cell sub-
classes, including both excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subdivi-
sions, were subjected to EWCE in each subregion and developmental
stage, provided they contained 100 or more cells. This analysis allowed
us to discern which cell populations in the developing human fore-
brain disproportionately express known disease-risk genes.
Derivation of NSCs from human PSCs
Culture and differentiation of hNSCs were performed and described in
Micali et al.40. Brieﬂy, forebrain NSCs were generated from human
embryonic stem cells (hESC) line H9 and then serially passaged in
20 ng/mL FGF2 from passage (PS)2 to PS8. Human NSCs from each
passage were exposed to 0.1, 1, 10 and 20 ng/mL FGF2 for 6 days to
assess their differentiation trajectory, before RNA extraction and bulk
RNA-seq analysis (NSC progression protocol). The six human iPSC lines
(2063-1, 2; 2053-2, 6, 2075-1, 3) were differentiated into forebrain NSCs.
hNSCs were passaged on DIV 8, then neuronal differentiation started
on DIV 12. On DIV 17, hNSCs were passaged over astrocytes or without
astrocytes and terminally differentiated into neurons until DIV
32 (Neuronal differentiation protocol). In the current work, we have
re-analyzed those data focusing on hNSCs differentiated without
astrocytes and the DIV 8, 17 and 30 RNA-seq samples.
Comparison of disease-associated gene expression in human
primary RG cells and in vitro NSCs
To determine the fraction of disease-associated genes expressed in
early RG cells from human ﬁrst-trimester brain versus hNSCs in vitro,
we compared their abundance in the scRNA-seq data from Braun
et al.44 and in bulk RNA-seq data from human PSC-derived NSCs
sequentially passaged in different FGF2 dose, reported in Micali et al.40.

strength of that pattern in each sample. “A” is the amplitude matrix
with genes as rows and patterns as columns, with values indicating the
strength of involvement of a given gene in each pattern. In this way, the

Gene regulatory network analysis of bulk RNA-seq data using
RcisTarget
We leveraged RcisTarget (version 1.18.2)110 to build gene regulatory
networks based on motif enrichment analysis within gene lists. We
generated sets of genes using two criteria: (1) grouping genes by their
associated diseases, which yielded disease regulons, and (2) grouping
genes by their expression peak across in vitro hNSC progression from
Micali et al.40, yielding temporal regulons. In the lists of disease genes,
one gene can be associated with more than one disease. In the case of
the expression-peak list, a gene can only be assigned to one group.
RcisTarget searches for enrichment of TF binding motifs using a pre-
calculated database of binding motifs in gene ﬂanking sequences
(database version: v10 – human). RcisTarget was set up to identify
motifs in the ﬂanking sequences (up to 10 kb around the gene
transcription-start site, TSS) and we used a threshold of normalized
enrichment score of 3. From the output of RcisTarget, we selected only
TFs labeled as “high conﬁdence”. Finally, we determined a network
qualiﬁed as a regulon if the core TF was also included in the input list
used for computing the network. Genes not expressed in the in vitro
system were excluded from the analysis.
For each disease list that resulted in at least one regulon, we
generated 1000 random lists of genes, each containing the same
number of genes as the original list, that were tested using RcisTarget.
We counted the occurrences of every TF in the core TFs of the random
results. We then determined the permutation p-value of the core TFs
observed in the original lists, calculated as the proportion of random
lists in which the TF was identiﬁed as core TF.
Since genes in the same disease list are not necessarily
co-expressed, we tested the expression correlation between core TFs
and their target genes using the hNSC dataset from Micali et al.40. The
biweight midcorrelations (Student test p-value) was computed with
the WGCNA R package’s bicorAndPvalue111 function (version 1.72-1)
across 20 samples (PS2, PS3, PS4, PS6, PS8; and 20, 10, 1, 0.1 ng/mL
FGF2 for each passage). Then, we counted the number of genes in each
regulon that were signiﬁcantly correlated (positively and negatively)
with each core TF. The number of targets signiﬁcantly correlated with a
regulon was validated with another permutation strategy. That is, we
created random lists of target genes matching the number of target
genes in the regulons and maintaining the proportion of genes peaking
at each passage and FGF2 concentration. For each list of random target
genes, we computed the expression correlations and the number of
correlated targets, as described above. We used the distribution of
random targets signiﬁcantly correlated with the core TF to determine
the permutation p-value of our results, and corrected for multiple
comparisons using the BH method.
To characterize the expression dynamics of each disease reg-
ulon, we analyzed their target genes and visualized the distribution
of expression bias across three contexts: RG cell-to-neuron differ-
entiation (using data from Telley et al.57), subtype expression bias in
maturing cortical projection neurons (from the DeCoN dataset),
and dorso-ventral expression bias in NSC lines (based on Micali
et al.40).

Reannotation of human RG cells from Trevino et al.62 scRNA-seq
dataset
ScRNA-seq data of the prenatal human cortex from four donors,
PCW16, 20, 21, and 24 from Trevino et al.62 were obtained from the
Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE162170. We used scanpy
(version 1.10.4)113 to preprocess the expression data. We retained
cells with less than 10% mitochondrial counts and genes with at least
one count. This resulted in a dataset of 53,231 cells and 27,886
expressed genes. To classify cell-cycle phases in each cell, we scored
the expression of cell-cycle phase-associated genes114 and classiﬁed
cells based on these genes. Next, we identiﬁed highly variable genes
within each donor and selected the top 5,000 genes. We normalized
the data to a value of 10000 counts per cell, log-transformed it, and
scaled it. To model gene expression and integrate data across sam-
ples, we employed scVI (version 0.19.0)115, a deep generative model
for scRNA-seq data analysis. We used the sequencing batch as a batch
variable and included mitochondrial and ribosomal count fractions
as covariates, as well as cell cycle scores. The latent space size was set
to 10, and we obtained corresponding embeddings for all cells in the
preprocessed data.
To further deﬁne early cell types present in the dataset, we
selected progenitors (cycling, multipotent glial precursor cells
(mGPCs), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) and neuronal
intermediate precursor cells (nIPCs) and early, late, and truncated RG
cells. We used 15 nearest neighbors in the embedding space, created
an UMAP representation, and identiﬁed cell clusters using the Leiden
algorithm. Using a selection of known marker genes from Micali
et al.37 and Trevino et al.62, we assigned cell type identities based on
clusters’ gene expression and excluded a low-count RG cluster (LQ
RG), ependymal cells and interneurons. We could identify and label
ventricular (v), truncated (t), and outer (o) RG cells, as well as early
neurons, nIPCs, mGPCs, OPCs and astrocytes. Finally, in order to
distinguish early from late states in both vRG and oRG clusters, we
subclustered RG cells based on the marker genes of the mouse RG
temporal progression from Telley et al.57, which are distinguished as
early (gene modules “prog_2” and “prog_3”), mid (“prog_4”) and late
(“prog_5” and “prog_6”). We chose this mouse dataset because mice
possess a small proportion of oRG cells, therefore the early to late
gene modules could reﬂect RG maturation rather than transcrip-
tional changes from vRG to oRG cells. We found that this early-to-late
gene signature was shared between vRG and oRG cells, and we used it
to classify early and late vRG (vRG E and vRG L) and oRG (oRG E and
oRG L) cells.
In silico TF knock-out simulations in scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq
data using CellOracle
We leveraged CellOracle (version 0.12.0)63 to simulate the impact of
the perturbation of TFs on the transcriptome of each cell type along
the progression of human NSCs, neurogenesis and gliogenesis, using
the reannotated data from Trevino et al.62. We considered vRG E and
vRG L, tRG, oRG E and oRG L, as well as mGPCs, astrocytes and OPCs of
all donors (PCW16, 20, 21, and 24) to obtain a representative dataset of
the progression of RG cells and gliogenic differentiation. To analyze
the neurogenic trajectories, we pulled RG cell clusters, except tRG
cells, which are late progenitors and might have reduced neurogenic
potential116, and considered nIPCs, early neurons and glutamatergic
neurons, from each donor separately. We obtained three data subsets
of neurogenesis at PCW 20, 21, and 24, and one subset of RG pro-
gression and gliogenesis comprising all ages. We conducted CellOracle
perturbation analysis in each of the data subsets: RG progression/
gliogenesis, and neurogenesis PCW20, PCW21 and PCW24. PCW16
donor was not included in the neurogenic lineage since we could not
obtain a clear trajectory from NSCs towards differentiated cells in the
cell diffusion maps.
First, we preprocessed the data as suggested in the CellOracle
pipeline. In brief, genes with 0 counts were removed, count data was
normalized per cell and only the 3000 top highly variable genes were
used. Then, data were normalized again, log-transformed and scaled.
We embedded cells in UMAP, PHATE (version 1.0.10)117 and ForceAtlas2
(version 0.3.5)118 2D-maps based on the scVI 10-dimensional embed-
dings computed previously and chose the dimensionality reduction
that best ﬁts with each trajectory. In the case of the neurogenic subsets
from individual donors, PHATE maps were produced (knn: 100, phate
decay: 15, t: “auto”). In the RG progression/gliogenesis subset we ﬁrst
computed a diffusion map (knn: 10, number of components: 20) to
then generate a ForceAtlas2 map from it (knn: 50). K nearest neighbors
(knn) was selected as the pseudotime model to ﬁt in CellOracle.
Second, sample-matched scATAC-seq data from the same study
were leveraged to reconstruct a base gene regulatory network (GRN)
speciﬁc to each subset of the dataset. Monocle3 (version 1.3.7)119 was
used to preprocess the data using latent semantic indexing (LSI) as
the normalization method. Peaks and peak-to-peak co-accessibility
were obtained by Cicero (version 1.3.9)120. Peaks overlapping a TSS
were annotated to the corresponding gene and only those peaks with
a co-accessibility greater than 0.8 were retained. Peaks were scanned
for motifs using CellOracle’s scan function, which uses the gimme-
motifs (version 0.17.0)121 motif scanner (false positive rate: 0.02,
default motif database: gimme.vertebrate.v5.0 using binding and
inferred motifs, and cumulative binding score cutoff: 8) to generate
an annotated peak-motif binary matrix. This subset-speciﬁc base

speciﬁc links were retrieved by ﬁtting the GRN to the cell-type-
speciﬁc expression matrix using a bagging ridge regression model
(bagging_number: 20, alpha: 10). The links in the resulting networks
were ﬁltered by p-value (p-value < 0.001) and from those, only the
top 2000 links were retained based on their mean coefﬁcients. After
this ﬁltering, the model was ﬁt once more to adjust the coefﬁcients of
the preserved links.

developmental ﬂow from the data. We manually selected the following
parameters in the CellOracle pipeline: ridge alpha: 10, mass smooth
factor: 0.8, grid points: 40, scale of the ﬂow: 40. To avoid empty grid
points, the knn and “min_p_mass” ﬁlter values were adjusted in each

Transcriptome and GRN complexity
We compared transcriptome and GRN complexity in different cell
types across human neurogenesis (at PCW 20, 21 and 24) and RG cell
progression and gliogenesis (all donors) from Trevino et al.62. Tran-
scriptome complexity was assessed using several metrics calculated
for all TFs in each cell type122. The number of expressed TFs in each cell
type was quantiﬁed as the total number of TFs with detectable
expression (non-zero expression levels) in that cell type. To evaluate
the diversity and evenness of transcript expression, we computed
Shannon entropy (H): H = -∑i pi log2(pi), where pi is the proportion of
total transcript expression contributed by a TF. We also calculated
Simpson’s diversity index: D = 1-∑i pi
2, which reﬂects the probability
that two transcripts randomly chosen from the dataset belong to dif-
ferent TFs. Additionally, the coefﬁcient of variation (CV), deﬁned as the
ratio of the standard deviation (σ) to the mean (µ) expression, was
calculated for all TFs in each cell type as CV = σ/µ. Complexity of cell-
type-speciﬁc GRNs was evaluated using metrics computed by Cel-
lOracle. These metrics included degree (all), representing the total
number of connections (incoming and outgoing) for each gene, and
degree centrality (all), quantifying the relative importance of genes
based on their total degree. Degree (in) and degree (out) capture the
number of incoming and outgoing connections for each gene, repre-
senting the number of upstream regulators and downstream target
genes, respectively. Additional metrics included betweenness cen-
trality, measuring how often a TF lies on the shortest paths between
other genes, and eigenvector centrality, which evaluates the inﬂuence
of a TF based on the importance of its neighbors. Connectivity was
used to distinguish intra-modular connectivity (connections within the
same gene module) from global connectivity (connections across
modules). Finally, participation measures the extent to which a TF is
connected to multiple modules within the network.
Disease-gene enrichment in CellOracle’s cell-type speciﬁc GRNs
We computed the enrichment of disease-associated genes within TF
target sets using the ﬁsher.test function in R. Target gene lists of every
TF were derived from cell-type-speciﬁc gene regulatory networks
constructed by CellOracle in the neurogenesis (PCW 20, 21, and 24)
and RG cell progression and gliogenesis datasets from Trevino et al.62.
We used the set of highly variable genes identiﬁed within each subset
as the background set for the test. For contingency tables containing
zero counts, the Haldane correction was applied by adding 0.5 to all
categories. The analysis provided the fraction of genes associated with
each disease in the regulon, the odds ratio of the enrichment, and the
corresponding p-value. P-values were adjusted for multiple testing by
controlling the False Discovery Rate (FDR) using the BH method. We
corrected p-values of all TFs tested at three levels: in each dataset, in
each dataset and disease combination, and in each dataset, disease and
cell type combination. Results with an FDR-adjusted p-value ≤0.05 at
the most granular level (dataset-disease-cell type combinations) were
considered signiﬁcant.

states: RG cells, IPCs, and neurons. After CellOracle’s simulations, we
counted the number of IPCs that transitioned into RG cells (earlier

comparisons between donors of the fraction of IPCs that transitioned
into RG cells or neurons using a linear regression. We also tested the
number of gene knockouts with a coincident effect (“to progenitor” or
“to mature neuron”) across donors using a Fisher’s test.

Differential expression analysis between ASD and control
groups in pseudo-bulk RGEarly from scRNA-seq data
We performed differential expression analysis between ASD and con-
trol grouped samples on pseudo-bulk samples generated from the
scRNA-seq data of RGEarly cluster, the most abundant cell type in the
data and in all donors. The approach we followed to create pseudo-
bulk samples was modiﬁed from He et al.126. Brieﬂy, we ﬁrst divided
RGEarly by cell cycle phase and donor. All cells were embedded into a
common neighbor graph using Seurat’s FindNeighbors function (ver-
sion 5.1.0). Then, in each donor and cell cycle phase combination, we
selected 3 cells at random, named capitals. This was the number of
desired pseudo-bulk samples per group to obtain. The distances in the
neighbor graph to these capitals were measured for all cells in the
group and they were assigned to the closest capital. We ﬁlled the
capitals until the desired number of cells per sample was reached, i.e.,
314 cells. This number corresponds to the minimum number of cells
per donor and cell cycle phase combination divided by the number of
samples we wanted to create. Finally, for each capital, the raw counts
from all cells assigned to it were aggregated into a single pseudo-bulk
sample. We visualized the variation present in these data using PCA.
We performed differential expression testing between the ASD and
control groups using DESeq2105. Speciﬁcally, we employed a Wald test
and we included condition (ASD or control), cell cycle phase and donor
as variables in the expression model, as well as the interaction between
phase and condition. Genes with an BH-adjusted p-value < 0.05 and an
absolute log2FC > 0.5 were considered differentially expressed. To
represent the results, we constructed a volcano plot displaying log2FC
and adjusted p-value, labeling signiﬁcant genes with adjusted
p-value < 10^-12.5 or in the top 30 genes by absolute log2FC. Addi-

signiﬁcant DEGs using all genes tested, by means of a one-sided
Fisher’s exact test. Imprinted human genes were obtained from the
National Center for Biotechnology Information database geneim-
print.com, and we considered imprinted genes those labeled as
“Imprinted” in the database.

25 mg/mL insulin, 30 nM sodium selenite, 1x Glutamax (Life Technol-

10 ng/mL NT-3 (R&D Systems, 267-N3) until day 38. Bulk RNA was
collected on day 8, 17, 32, 38, using RNAeasy mini kit (Qiagen).
Single-cell dissociation of ASD and control NSCs
The differentiation protocol for control (#290, #311, #317) and idio-
pathic ASD (#375, #384, #434) iPSC-derived NSCs is described above.
At DIV8, all NSC lines cultured in N2 + B27 + XLSB at 37 °C and 20% O2
in 24-well plates were dissociated using 500 µL Accutase per well,
diluted 1:1 in N2, and incubated for 5-10 minutes at 37 °C. Cells were
detached from 2-3 wells per condition, collected in 15 mL tubes, and
diluted with 5 mL N2. After centrifugation at 180g (1000 RPM) for
5 min, the pellets were resuspended in 5 mL N2 to remove residual
Accutase, centrifuged again, and resuspended in 1-2 mL HBSS. Single-
cell suspensions were prepared by gentle pipetting with a 1 mL
micropipette, followed by ﬁltration through 40 µm cell strainers (Fal-
con, 352340). Cell counts were performed using an automatic cell
counter (ThermoFisher Scientiﬁc). Samples with at least 90% of cell
viability were processed for RNAseq. Cell suspensions were diluted in
HBSS to 1000 cells/µL and processed for single-cell RNA-seq analysis
within 20 minutes at the Yale Center for Genome Analysis (YCGA) core
facility.
Construction of 10X Genomic Single Cell 3’ RNA-Seq libraries
and sequencing
The preparation of the single cell suspension from cultured NSCs
derived from control and ASD iPSCs is described above.
GEM Generation and Barcoding. Single cell suspension in RT
Master Mix is loaded on the Single Cell A Chip and partition with a pool
of about 750,000 barcoded gel beads to form nanoliter-scale Gel
Beads-In-Emulsions (GEMs). Each gel bead has primers containing (i)
an Illumina® R1 sequence (read 1 sequencing primer), (ii) a 16 nt 10x
Barcode, (iii) a 12 nt Unique Molecular Identiﬁer (UMI), and (iv) a poly-
dT primer sequence (30nt). Upon dissolution of the Gel Beads in a
GEM, the primers are released and mixed with cell lysate and Master
Mix. Incubation of the GEMs then produces barcoded, full-length
cDNA from poly-adenylated mRNA.
Post GEM-RT Cleanup, cDNA Ampliﬁcation and library construc-
tion. Silane magnetic beads are used to remove leftover biochemical
reagents and primers from the post-GEM reaction mixture. Full-length,
barcoded cDNA is then ampliﬁed by PCR to generate sufﬁcient mass
for library construction. Enzymatic Fragmentation and Size Selection
are used to optimize the cDNA amplicon size prior to library con-
struction. R1 (read 1 primer sequence) are added to the molecules
during GEM incubation. P5, P7, a sample index, and R2 (read 2 primer
sequence) are added during library construction via End Repair,
A-tailing, Adaptor Ligation, and PCR. The ﬁnal libraries contain the P5
and P7 primers used in Illumina bridge ampliﬁcation.
Sequencing libraries. The Single Cell 3’ Protocol produces
Illumina-ready sequencing libraries. A Single Cell 3’ Library com-
prises standard Illumina paired-end constructs which begin and end
with P5 and P7. The Single Cell 3’ 16 bp 10x Barcode and 12 bp UMI
are encoded in Read 1, while Read 2 is used to sequence the cDNA
fragment (91 bp). Sequencing a Single Cell 3’ Library produces a
standard Illumina BCL data output folder. The BCL data will include
the paired-end Read 1 (containing the 16 bp 10x™Barcode and 12 bp
UMI) and Read 2 and the sample index in the i7 index read. Minimum
sequencing depth is 20,000 read pairs per cell. This dataset is fully
available.
Bulk RNA-sequencing library preparation
At the time points across the in vitro culture indicated in Supple-
mentary Fig. 25a, b, total RNA was extracted from 3 different wells/
conditions of the NSCs derived from ASD and Control lines, using
RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, 74104), according to the manufacturer’s
protocol.
RNA Seq Quality Control: Total RNA quality was determined by
estimating the A260/A280 and A260/A230 ratios by nanodrop. RNA
integrity was determined by running an Agilent Bioanalyzer gel, which
measures the ratio of the ribosomal peaks. Samples with RIN values of
7 or greater were considered for library prep.
RNA Seq Library Prep: mRNA was puriﬁed from approximately
200 ng of total RNA with oligo-dT beads and sheared by incubation at
94 °C in the presence of Mg (Roche Kapa mRNA Hyper Prep Cat.
KR1352). Following ﬁrst-strand synthesis with random primers, second
strand synthesis and A-tailing were performed with dUTP for gen-
erating strand-speciﬁc sequencing libraries. Adapter ligation with 3’
dTMP overhangs were ligated to library insert fragments. Library
ampliﬁcation ampliﬁes fragments carrying the appropriate adapter
sequences at both ends. Strands marked with dUTP were not ampli-
ﬁed. Indexed libraries were quantiﬁed by qRT-PCR using a commer-
cially available kit (Roch KAPA Biosystems Cat. KK4854) and insert size
distribution determined by either the Agilent Bioanalyzer. Samples
with a yield of ≥0.5 ng/ul and a size distribution of 150-300 bp were
used for sequencing.
Flow Cell Preparation and Sequencing: Sample concentrations
were normalized to 1.2 nM and loaded onto an Illumina NovaSeq ﬂow
cell at a concentration that yields 25 million passing ﬁlter clusters per
sample. Samples were sequenced using 100 bp paired-end sequencing
on an Illumina NovaSeq6000 according to Illumina protocols. The
10 bp unique dual index was read during additional sequencing reads
that automatically follow the completion of read 1. Data generated
during sequencing runs were simultaneously transferred to the YCGA
high-performance computing cluster. A positive control (prepared
bacteriophage Phi X library) provided by Illumina was spiked into
every lane at a concentration of 0.3% to monitor sequencing quality in
real time.

Animals
Rhesus macaques (macaca mulatta) were bred in Rakic primate
breeding colony at the Yale Animal Resources Center. Timed pregnant
females, between 4 and 10 years old, underwent caesarian (c) section
at the indicated embryonic age (E), performed by Yale’s Veterinary
Clinical Services (VCS), as previously reported37. Monkeys were seda-
ted with ketamine (3 mg/kg) and atropine sulfate (Lily, 0.2 mg/kg). A
midline incision was made in the abdominal wall and the uterus
exposed through the opening. The uterus was then incised between
the primary and secondary lobes of the discoid placenta, the chor-
ioallantoic membrane was punctured and the fetus delivered,
decapitated still under the effects of anesthesia from maternal blood.
The head of the fetus was transported to an adjacent room housing a
BSL2 hood, brain was collected and ﬁxed in paraformaldehyde (PFA).
Post-operatively, the animals were monitored several times a day until
full recovery.
Fixation and sectioning of the brain tissue
Rhesus macaque fetal brains were dissected and immersed ﬁxed in 4%
paraformaldehyde (PFA) overnight. Fixed brains were dehydrated in
step-gradients of up to 30% sucrose/PBS (Sigma-Aldrich, S0389) for
2–3 days at 4 °C, then embedded in OCT (Leica, 3801480) and frozen at
−80 °C. Sagittal sections were prepared at 25 µm on a Leica CM3050S
cryostat and stored at −80 ° until use. The sex of the fetuses was not
considered for the imaging analyses.
RNAscope
Single-molecule RNA in situ hybridizations were performed by
Advanced Cell Diagnostics, Newark, CA, using RNAscopeTM technol-
ogy. Paired double-Z oligonucleotide probes were designed against
target RNA using custom software. All probes used in this study are
shown in Supplementary Dataset 12. RNAscope LS Fluorescent Multi-
plex Kit (Advanced Cell Diagnostics, Newark, CA, 322800) was used
with custom pretreatment conditions following the instruction man-
ual. Fixed frozen fetal macaque brain tissue slides were manually post-
ﬁxed in 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) at room temperature for
90 minutes. Then the slides were dehydrated in a series of ethanols
and loaded onto the Leica Bond RX automated stainer, performing the
reagent changes, starting with the pretreatments (protease), followed
by the probe incubation, ampliﬁcation steps, ﬂuorophores, and DAPI
counterstain. RNAscope 2.5 LS Protease III was used for 15 minutes at
40 °C. Pretreatment conditions were optimized for each sample and
quality control for RNA integrity was completed using probes speciﬁc
to the housekeeping genes Polr2a, Ppib, and Ubc, which are low,
moderate, and high-expressing genes, respectively. Negative control
background staining was evaluated using a probe speciﬁc to the bac-
terial dapB gene. Coverslipping was done manually using ProLong
Gold mounting media at the end of each run. The RNAscope analysis
shown in Fig. 2c–e was performed on one fetus at E40 and one at E52.
Immunohistochemistry
Fixed frozen monkey fetal brain tissue slides were re-hydrated in PBS.
Sections were blocked overnight at 4 °C, in PBS containing 10% donkey
serum (Jackson Immunoresearch, 017-000-121) and 0.3% Triton X-100
(Sigma-Aldrich, T8787), then incubated with primary anti-DMRTA1
(1:100; Abcam, ab238679), anti-FEZF2 (1:50; Sigma-Aldrich, ABN428),
anti-HES1 (1:500; Cell Signaling, 11988), anti-LHX2 (1:100; Santacruz, sc-
19344), anti-PAX6 (1:200; R&D Systems, AF8150), anti-POU3F2 (1:200;
Abcam, ab137469), anti-SOX2 (1:200; R&D Systems, MAB2018), or anti-
YBX3 (1:200; Abcam, ab251828) antibodies for 12 hours at 4 °C. Sodium
citrate antigen retrieval was performed before using anti-FEZF2 and
anti-YBX3 antibodies. Slides were immersed in 10 mM sodium citrate
buffer (pH 6.0; Sigma-Aldrich, S4641) with 0.01% Tween-20 (Thomas
Scientiﬁc, C987C36) and microwaved for 20 min, followed by cooling
at room temperature for 30 min. After incubation with the primary
antibodies, four washes with PBS containing 0.1% Tween-20 were
performed. Then, the sections were incubated at 4 °C for 12 h with
secondary antibodies conjugated to FITC, Cy3, and Cy5 (1:400; Jackson
Immunoresearch). Nuclei were stained for 10 min with DAPI (1 µg/mL,
Sigma-Aldrich, D9542) at room temperature and then slides were
mounted in Prolong Gold Antifade Mountant (Invitrogen, P36930).
The immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis shown in Fig. 5g was per-
formed on one E44 rhesus macaque fetus. IHC was repeated three
times for each antibody.
Microscopy and imaging
Panoramics of the ﬂuorescent monkey brain tissue slices were
acquired using Zeiss Axioscan 7, equipped with cameras Axiocam 705
color and Orca Flash 4.0 V3, or the slide scanner (Olympus, VS200).
High-resolution z-stack images were captured using a Zeiss LSM800
confocal microscope, or a Zeiss 510 Meta confocal microscope. Z-stack
and tiled images were processed using Zeiss ZEN2009 and ImageJ
(version 2.0.0-rc-69/1.52p). Slight artefactual defects of DAPI intensity
were manually corrected with ImageJ. When necessary, ﬂuorescence
intensity or contrast was slightly adjusted using consistent parameters
for all the specimens using Image J, ZEN acquisition software version
2018, or QuPath (version 0.4.4).
